concepts.name: Evolution of E-waste Rules in India: 2011 → 2016 → 2022
key_dimensions: Key shifts from 2011 to 2016 rules (inclusion of CFL/mercury-containing lamps, expanded producer list)
Major changes in 2022 rules (PRO-based system replaced by EPR portal, new categories added)
Why 2016 rules were amended — implementation gaps and informal sector issues
UPSC trap: Which iteration first introduced Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) — 2011 rules

concepts.name: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) under E-waste Rules
key_dimensions: Definition and legal basis of EPR under E-waste (Management) Rules, 2022
Shift from physical EPR (take-back schemes) to market-based EPR (EPR certificates/credits)
Obligations of Producers, Importers, and Brand Owners (PIBOs) under EPR framework
UPSC trap: EPR certificates are tradeable — distinguishing this from other waste rules where EPR is not certificate-based

concepts.name: Scope and Coverage: What Constitutes E-waste under Indian Rules
key_dimensions: Definition of e-waste under Rule 3 of E-waste (Management) Rules, 2022
Schedule I: Categories of Electrical and Electronic Equipment (EEE) covered (IT, telecom, consumer equipment, etc.)
What is EXCLUDED: radioactive waste, waste from military/paramilitary establishments
UPSC trap: E-waste rules do NOT cover all electronic items — exemptions and boundary conditions

concepts.name: Roles and Responsibilities of Key Stakeholders
key_dimensions: Producers' obligations: EPR targets, registration on portal, annual returns
Dealers and refurbishers: deposit e-waste to authorized dismantlers/recyclers
Consumers (bulk and individual): channelize e-waste only to authorized entities
UPSC trap: Refurbishers are explicitly recognized as a stakeholder category — unique to 2022 rules

concepts.name: EPR Targets and Collection Mechanism under 2022 Rules
key_dimensions: EPR targets are now expressed as a percentage of EEE placed on market in previous years (phased targets)
Centralized online EPR portal managed by CPCB for registration and certificate trading
Concept of 'EPR Certificate' — generated by registered recyclers, purchased by producers
UPSC trap: Targets are based on weight of EEE sold, not units — distinction matters for calculations

concepts.name: Role of Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) vs. State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs)
key_dimensions: CPCB: Manages EPR portal, grants authorization to recyclers/dismantlers at national level, publishes guidelines
SPCBs/PCCs: Grant authorization to collection centers, dismantlers, and recyclers at state level
CPCB's power to impose Environmental Compensation (EC) for non-compliance
UPSC trap: Registration of PIBOs is with CPCB (central portal), NOT with SPCBs — common confusion point

concepts.name: Authorization and Registration Framework for Recyclers and Dismantlers
key_dimensions: Distinction between 'dismantler' and 'recycler' — separate categories requiring separate authorization
Conditions for grant, renewal, and suspension of authorization by SPCBs
Refurbishers require separate registration — a new addition in 2022 rules
UPSC trap: PRO (Producer Responsibility Organization) model phased out in 2022 — no longer an authorized channel

concepts.name: Environmental Compensation (EC) Mechanism
key_dimensions: EC replaces the earlier penalty-based approach — polluter pays principle operationalized
CPCB has power to levy EC on producers failing to meet EPR targets
EC funds are deposited in an 'Environmental Compensation Fund' managed by CPCB
UPSC trap: EC is not a 'fine' under criminal law — it is an administrative charge; different from penalties under EPA 1986

concepts.name: Informal Sector and E-waste: Policy Recognition and Integration
key_dimensions: India's informal sector handles ~95% of e-waste but is largely unregulated and hazardous
2022 rules attempt to integrate informal sector through formalization pathways for dismantlers
Health hazards to informal workers: acid bath processes, open burning releasing dioxins/furans
UPSC trap: Rules do not directly 'legalize' informal sector — they create incentives for formalization, not amnesty

concepts.name: Scheduled Items and Categories: EEE Schedules in 2022 Rules
key_dimensions: Schedule I lists categories of EEE (e.g., IT equipment, telecom, consumer electronics, solar panels added in 2022)
Schedule II: Restricted Hazardous Substances (RoHS) — lead, mercury, cadmium, hexavalent chromium, PBB, PBDE
Threshold concentration values for restricted substances
UPSC trap: Solar photovoltaic panels included in 2022 rules — NOT covered under earlier rules; a high-yield addition

concepts.name: Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) Provisions
key_dimensions: RoHS provisions restrict use of specific substances in new EEE placed on market
Six substances restricted under Schedule II with maximum concentration thresholds
Exemptions to RoHS: certain medical devices, military equipment, spare parts for equipment sold before rules
UPSC trap: RoHS is a MANUFACTURING regulation (upstream), while EPR is a POST-CONSUMER regulation (downstream) — different points of intervention

concepts.name: E-waste Rules and Parent Legislation: Environment Protection Act, 1986
key_dimensions: E-waste Rules are framed under Section 6, 8, and 25 of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986
EPA 1986 is the umbrella legislation — e-waste rules derive their penal power from EPA
Penalties for violation: imprisonment up to 5 years or fine up to ₹1 lakh or both (under EPA)
UPSC trap: The E-waste Rules themselves do not prescribe imprisonment — penalties flow from EPA 1986, not directly from the rules

concepts.name: Deposit Refund System (DRS) and Financial Instruments for E-waste
key_dimensions: Concept of DRS: consumers pay deposit at purchase, refunded when returning e-waste
DRS not yet mandatorily implemented in India but discussed as a future instrument in policy documents
Comparison with global models: Germany's take-back mandate, Japan's Home Appliance Recycling Law
UPSC trap: 2022 rules do NOT mandate DRS — it is a policy recommendation, not a legal obligation yet

concepts.name: E-waste and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Linkages
key_dimensions: SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption and Production): Target 12.4 on hazardous waste management
SDG 3 (Good Health): E-waste releases toxic substances linked to health outcomes in informal workers
Urban Mining concept: e-waste as a secondary resource for gold, silver, palladium — circular economy link
UPSC trap: Urban mining is not regulated under E-waste Rules per se — it falls under broader mineral policy and EPR framework

concepts.name: Transboundary Movement of E-waste: Basel Convention and India's Position
key_dimensions: Basel Convention on the Control of Transboundary Movements of Hazardous Wastes (1989) — India a party
Basel Ban Amendment (2019 enforcement): prohibits export of hazardous e-waste from developed to developing nations
India's Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management) Rules, 2016 govern transboundary movement alongside e-waste rules
UPSC trap: E-waste import for refurbishment is conditionally allowed in India — but export of e-waste is prohibited; direction matters

concepts.name: Producer Responsibility Organizations (PROs): Rise and Phase-out
key_dimensions: PROs were introduced in 2016 rules as collective compliance bodies — producers could meet EPR through PROs
2022 rules abolished the PRO model in favor of direct producer accountability via CPCB EPR portal
Rationale for phase-out: PROs created accountability gaps, lack of transparency in e-waste channelization
UPSC trap: PROs still exist in Plastic Waste Management Rules 2016 (amended 2022) — do NOT confuse with e-waste rules where they are phased out

concepts.name: E-waste Rules vs. Other Waste Management Rules: Key Distinctions
key_dimensions: E-waste vs. Hazardous Waste Rules: overlapping jurisdiction for CRTs, batteries — boundary conditions
E-waste vs. Battery Waste Management Rules 2022: batteries in EEE governed by Battery Waste Rules when separated
E-waste vs. Plastic Waste Rules: plastic components of e-waste — which rule governs?
UPSC trap: When e-waste contains hazardous components AND is subject to another rule, E-waste Rules take precedence for the whole item — but separated components revert to their respective rules

concepts.name: Annual Reporting, Audit, and Compliance Mechanism
key_dimensions: Producers must file annual returns on CPCB's EPR portal by a specified date
Third-party audit of e-waste recyclers and dismantlers mandated under 2022 rules
EPR certificate-based system creates a digital audit trail — transparency improvement over 2016 rules
UPSC trap: Under 2016 rules, annual returns were filed with SPCBs; under 2022 rules, filing is centralized with CPCB — a structural shift

concepts.name: E-waste Generation Data and India's Position Globally
key_dimensions: Global E-waste Monitor: India is the 3rd largest e-waste generator globally (after China and USA)
India generates ~3.2 million metric tonnes (MT) of e-waste annually (as per recent estimates)
Only ~22% of global e-waste is formally recycled — India's formal recycling rate is even lower
UPSC trap: India being 3rd in generation does NOT mean 3rd in per capita — per capita e-waste is much lower than developed nations

concepts.name: Solar Panel E-waste: New Frontier under 2022 Rules
key_dimensions: 2022 rules for the first time brought solar photovoltaic (PV) modules under e-waste regulation
Producers of solar panels now have EPR obligations — phased targets for collection and recycling
Significance: India's massive solar capacity addition (500 GW target by 2030) will generate enormous PV waste after 25-year lifespan
UPSC trap: Solar panels were NOT under e-waste rules before 2022 — this is a critical new addition frequently tested
